ruleIntents.intent: Checks that any element which actually overflows-and-scrolls its own content in the same document (CSS overflow producing a real scroll distance beyond padding) can be reached by Tab — i.e. either the scroll container itself is in the tab order (tabindex >= 0), OR some descendant in the flat tree is in the tab order (so focus can land inside the region), OR the region is inert (so it legitimately needs no keyboard reachability). The underlying concern: arrow keys only scroll a region when focus is on/inside it, so a scroll container with no tab stop on or within it is unreachable/unscrollable by keyboard-only users.
ruleIntents.scLimb: 2.1.1 Keyboard, specifically the "all functionality is operable through a keyboard interface" limb as applied to the scrolling operation. It targets the implicit interactive functionality of scrolling overflowing content (rather than activation of explicit controls like links/buttons). It does NOT exercise the "without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes" limb. It also maps to 2.1.3 (Keyboard No Exception, AAA), the same limb without the exception clause.
ruleIntents.applicability: Any HTML element with visible children in the flat tree where CSS produces a genuine scroll distance: horizontal scroll distance greater than computed left/right padding, OR vertical scroll distance greater than top/bottom padding. Requires DOM Tree + CSS Styling input aspects (computed overflow and scroll/padding metrics, not just markup). Explicitly excludes iframes/nested browsing contexts (the embedded document scrolls, tested by a separate rule). Not applicable when overflow is visible (scroll distance 0), hidden (not scrollable), content fits (no overflow), content is not visible, or the overflow is smaller than the padding.
ruleIntents.expectation: For each in-scope scrollable target, at least one is true: (a) the element itself is included in sequential focus navigation (e.g. tabindex="0"); or (b) it has a descendant in the flat tree included in sequential focus navigation (e.g. a contained <a href>/<button>); or (c) the element is inert. Any failed target => SC 2.1.1 not satisfied. All-passed or inapplicable => SC "needs further testing" (a pass here is not proof of conformance, because focus-on-region does not guarantee scripts let arrow keys reach the region, and decorative/whitespace/alternately-controlled scroll regions may fail the rule yet still meet the SC).
scenarioTypesPresent: PASS: scroll container itself focusable via tabindex=0 (vertical overflow)
PASS: container not focusable but contains a focusable descendant link in the flat tree
PASS: container made inert by an open modal <dialog>.showModal() (neither container nor descendants in tab order, scripted)
FAIL: vertically scrollable section with no tab stop on it or any descendant (overflow-y: scroll)
FAIL: horizontally scrollable image strip (overflow-y:auto + white-space:nowrap forcing horizontal overflow) with non-focusable children
INAPPLICABLE: overflow visible -> scroll distance 0
INAPPLICABLE: overflow auto but content fits -> scroll distance 0 in both directions
INAPPLICABLE: overflow hidden -> not scrollable
INAPPLICABLE: scrollable but no visible content (1px-tall spacer div)
INAPPLICABLE: scroll distance smaller than padding (padding-vs-scroll edge case)
INAPPLICABLE: iframe / nested browsing context (out of scope, scrolls embedded doc)
Near-duplicate variants differing only by linked URL (WCAG21 vs WCAG22 hrefs) for several of the above
syntheticNarrowness: Every case is a single bare <section> on an otherwise empty page; no surrounding tab order, no preceding/following focusable controls, no realistic page chrome (nav/header/footer) so 'reachable by sequential focus' is never tested against a long or competing tab sequence

Scrollable element is always a <section>; never tests scroll containers built from <div>, <ul>/<ol> lists, <pre> code blocks, <table> wrappers, <textarea>, chat logs, data grids, carousels, or framework components

Scroll is always created with plain CSS overflow:scroll/auto on a fixed px height/width; no flexbox/grid min-height:0 overflow, no max-height + overflow patterns, no dynamically-injected/AJAX-loaded content that becomes scrollable after load

The 'pass via focusable descendant' case relies on a single static <a href>; never covers descendants made focusable by tabindex, custom widgets, or focusable elements that are visually hidden/offscreen (which would be a deceptive pass)

Content is the same boilerplate WCAG abstract paragraph or a logo image strip every time; no real heterogeneous content, no nested scroll containers, no horizontally+vertically scrollable in the same element

The inert/pass case uses a contrived auto-opening modal dialog with leftover/broken script (references undefined myFrame) and a Chrome-internal ::backdrop selector, rather than a realistic inert pattern (inert attribute, aria-hidden subtree, off-canvas menu)

No coverage of the rule's own stated caveats: scripts that swallow arrow-key events (preventDefault on keydown), scroll controllable only via a custom button/scrollbar, or purely decorative scroll regions — all of which can fail/pass the rule but diverge from the actual SC outcome
tabindex test is binary (0 vs absent); never exercises negative tabindex (browser auto-focusable-but-not-sequential), positive tabindex reordering, or contenteditable/role overrides
Variety is largely illusory: several files are byte-near-duplicates differing only in WCAG21 vs WCAG22 in the href, inflating the apparent scenario count without adding distinct keyboard situations

Purely static HTML fixtures with no manual/dynamic Tab-then-Arrow verification, so a 'pass' only proves a tab stop exists, not that arrow keys actually scroll the region for a keyboard user (the SC's real-world question)

ruleIntents.intent: The rule checks a single, narrow structural defect: an `<iframe>` that contains keyboard-focusable interactive content must not be removed from the page's global tab-order by giving the iframe element itself a negative `tabindex`. The mechanism it targets is specific to nested browsing contexts: even when a control inside the iframe (e.g., a link) is itself in the iframe document's own sequential focus navigation order, a negative tabindex on the *iframe host element* excludes that entire inner focus scope from the flattened, page-level tabindex-ordered focus navigation scope, making the inner control unreachable by keyboard. Concretely it asserts: for any non-inert, content-bearing iframe, the iframe element's tabindex attribute value must not be a negative number.
ruleIntents.scLimb: SC 2.1.1 Keyboard — the "operable through a keyboard interface" limb, specifically the requirement that all functionality be reachable/available via sequential keyboard focus navigation. It exercises the focus-reachability (tab-order inclusion) aspect, not the keyboard-operability-once-focused aspect and not the "without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes" exception. It is the reachability sub-limb applied across a nested browsing-context boundary. (Also mapped to 2.1.3 Keyboard No Exception and Technique G202, but the in-scope requirement is 2.1.1.)
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any `iframe` element that is (a) not inert, and (b) contains at least one element that is BOTH visible AND part of the iframe document's own sequential focus navigation order. Containment is defined via the nested browsing context: the inner element's owner document is the iframe's container document. This deliberately excludes iframes whose inner content is non-focusable (e.g., only an `<h1>`), iframes hidden via `hidden`/zero-size so inner content is not visible, iframes whose only interactive content has been removed from the inner focus order (e.g., inner `tabindex='-1'`), and iframes that are inert (own `inert` attribute or blocked by an open modal `dialog` via `showModal()`).
ruleIntents.expectation: The test target (the applicable iframe element) does not have a negative number as its `tabindex` attribute value. Pass = no tabindex, or tabindex="0", or any non-negative value. Fail = tabindex is a negative number (e.g., "-1"). A failed outcome means SC 2.1.1 is not satisfied; a passed or inapplicable outcome means the SC needs further testing (the rule only catches this one exclusion mechanism, it does not affirm full keyboard accessibility).
scenarioTypesPresent: Passed: iframe with focusable inner content and NO tabindex attribute (default in-order)
Passed: iframe with focusable inner content and explicit tabindex="0"
Failed: iframe with focusable inner content and tabindex="-1" (the core violation)
Inapplicable: iframe whose inner content is non-focusable (only an <h1>)
Inapplicable: iframe hidden via the hidden attribute (inner content not visible)
Inapplicable: iframe shrunk to 1x1px (inner content not visible by size)
Inapplicable: inner interactive element itself removed from focus order via inner tabindex='-1'
Inapplicable: iframe made inert via its own inert attribute
Inapplicable: iframe dynamically made inert by an open modal dialog (showModal) plus JS-set tabindex=-1 (dynamic/scripted state)
syntheticNarrowness: Every applicable case uses the exact same single inner control: a one-line `Home` via srcdoc. No buttons, form fields, selects, textareas, contenteditable, custom widgets with tabindex='0', or multiple/nested focusable elements are ever tested.

The negative-tabindex value is only ever the literal "-1". Other negative values ("-2", "-99"), whitespace-padded (" -1 "), or non-integer/edge string forms that browsers still parse as negative are never exercised, even though the expectation is phrased generally as 'a negative number'.

All iframes are populated via the `srcdoc` attribute with trivial inline HTML. The far more common real-world case — an iframe loading a separate document via `src=` (same-origin or cross-origin third-party embeds like video players, maps, payment widgets, ad/social frames) — is entirely absent, including the cross-origin case where the inner focus order cannot even be statically inspected.

Only a single iframe per page is ever tested. No pages with multiple iframes, mixed pass/fail iframes on one page, or iframes nested inside other iframes (multi-level nested browsing contexts) appear.

Visibility/exclusion conditions are tested only in their cleanest synthetic form: `hidden` attribute and width/height=1. Real-world equivalents like CSS `display:none`/`visibility:hidden`, `opacity:0`, off-screen positioning, `aria-hidden`, zero-size via CSS rather than HTML attributes, or content covered by other elements are not represented, despite the rule depending on CSS Styling as a stated input aspect.

The 'inert via modal' dynamic scenario is overfit to one specific pattern (a `<dialog>` + `showModal()` that fires on DOMContentLoaded and simultaneously sets tabindex=-1). It is even duplicated nearly verbatim across two files. Other dynamic ways an iframe enters/leaves the tab-order at runtime (SPA route changes, lazy-loaded iframes, tabindex toggled by user interaction rather than on load, content injected after load) are not covered.

The 'inner content not focusable' inapplicable case is represented only by static markup (an <h1>, or a link with tabindex='-1'). Inner content that is focusable by default but disabled, or made non-focusable via scripting/ARIA, is not represented.

No test exercises the rule's stated Assumption boundary — interactive content that is keyboard-focusable but provides NO functionality (e.g., a button that does nothing). Per the rule, such a page can fail the rule yet still satisfy SC 2.1.1, but that nuanced true-fail-but-SC-satisfied situation has no test case.

All pages are minimal documents (a single iframe in an otherwise empty body) with no surrounding interactive context, so the rule's premise — that excluding the iframe breaks the *page's global/flattened* tab-order — is never demonstrated against a realistic page with other focusable elements before/after the iframe.

scLimbsCoveredByACT:
Core 'all functionality operable through a keyboard interface' — PARTIAL/narrow only. The corpus tests reachability via sequential focus navigation (tab order), which is a precondition of operability, through two thin slices: (a) Rule 0ssw9k — a scrollable region (or a focusable descendant) must be included in sequential focus navigation so arrow keys can scroll it (failed cases:
/ horizontally-scrolling sponsor logo strip with no tabbable descendant); (b) Rule akn7bn — an iframe containing visible, tab-order-participating interactive content (a link) must not be removed from the page tab-order via tabindex="-1" (failed case:

The 'keyboard interface' notion that focus order spans nested browsing contexts — akn7bn covers the flattened tabindex-ordered focus navigation scope, i.e. that iframe content participates in the page's global tab order (relevant to keyboard/AT/emulator reachability).

The inert/modal-dialog interaction with tab order — both rules include inert-driven inapplicable/pass cases (showModal() making a section or iframe inert; dialog backdrop; inert attribute), so 'content correctly removed from tab order when inert' is exercised as a non-failure condition.
scLimbsAbsentFromACT: Activation/operation of controls by keyboard — the entire heart of TT Test 4.A ('All functionality can be accessed AND EXECUTED using only the keyboard'). No test case requires pressing Enter/Space to activate a button, link, or control; both rules stop at focus/scroll reachability and never test that the focused thing actually does anything.
F54 failure pattern — pointing-device-only event handlers (e.g. , onclick-only) with no keyboard equivalent. Completely absent; no pointer-only handler appears in any of the 25 cases.

F42 failure pattern — emulated links/controls (scripted //
with onclick acting as a link) that cannot be tabbed to or activated by keyboard. Completely absent.
F55 failure pattern — script removing focus on receipt (onfocus="this.blur()", focus stolen back). Completely absent; no case tests that focus REMAINS on an element after it is received.

Custom interactive widgets implemented on non-interactive elements (div/span with role=button/menu/tab made keyboard-operable via tabindex + onkeydown) — the SCR29 advisory pattern. Absent; no custom-widget keyboard handling is tested.

Timing limb — TT Test 4.B / SC clause 'without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes' (repeated keystrokes in a short period, key held for an extended period, speed-dependent input). Entirely absent — zero coverage of any timing requirement.

Path-dependent exception — the SC's normative carve-out ('except where the underlying function requires input that depends on the path of the user's movement and not just the endpoints'): free-hand drawing, watercolor painting, helicopter simulator (Understanding Examples 4 and 5). No drawing/canvas/path-input case exists, so the exception is never exercised (neither a legitimately-exempt pass nor a wrongly-claimed exemption).

Essential information revealed only on hover/pointer (TT Test 4.A.2 / 4.A note: title/tooltip information that is essential must be reachable by keyboard or available elsewhere). Absent — no tooltip/hover-revealed-content case.

'Comparable / separate keyboard mode' alternative path (Understanding note: a separate keyboard mode, or a second keyboard-accessible method providing the same function, satisfies the SC; e.g. one of two print methods is keyboard accessible, or Understanding Example 7's pointer-only submit button passing because Enter submits the form). No alternative-path or redundant-mechanism case exists.

Keyboard emulators / alternate input devices and OS keyboard features — the Intent's coverage of speech input, sip-and-puff, on-screen keyboards, scanning software, and 'modifier key locking' not colliding; plus 'MouseKeys does not satisfy.' None of these device/AT considerations are represented (and could not be, given the corpus tests only DOM/CSS focusability).
Drag-and-drop with keyboard alternative (G90/G202 sufficient-technique pattern; Understanding Example 2 cut/paste alternative to drag). Absent.
Specific-timing-free keyboard alternative to a timing-dependent function (TT 4.B step 3). Absent.
contentDomainsPresent: Plain text article fragments — every 0ssw9k case is the same boilerplate 'WCAG 2.1 Abstract' heading + one paragraph of WCAG marketing prose inside a sized <section>.

Scrollable containers (CSS overflow scroll/auto/hidden/visible) with various padding, height/width, white-space:nowrap, and overflow axes — the only real 'UI pattern' variety, and it is CSS-property variation, not application variety.
A horizontally-scrolling image strip ('Our sponsors:') using logos (w3c-logo.png, eu-logo.svg) — the single image-bearing case.
iframes with srcdoc / src embedding a single link or an <h1>, sized normally, 1x1, hidden, or inert.

A modal <dialog> with showModal()/close() and a Cancel button, plus a trigger <button> — the only genuinely interactive control surface, and it appears only to drive the inert/inapplicable branch, not to be keyboard-activated.
Minimal inline <script> and inline style= / <style> blocks; lang="en"; no forms, no media beyond static logos, no canvas/SVG-interactivity, no ARIA widgets beyond a single role="heading".
varietyGaps: No FAILED case for the SC's central obligation: every failed case (3 total) is either 'scrollable region not focusable' or 'iframe taken out of tab order'. There is no failing page where a normal control (button/link/menu/form field/custom widget) cannot be operated by keyboard — i.e. the most common real-world 2.1.1 failure is unrepresented.

Control-type variety is near-zero: no native <button>/<a> activation test, no form inputs/select/checkbox/radio operability, no native <details>/<summary>, no menu/menubar, tabs, accordion, combobox, slider, or any ARIA composite widget. The only buttons present (dialog trigger/Cancel) exist solely to fire showModal() and are never keyboard-tested.

Event-handler variety is zero: not a single onclick/onmousedown/onkeydown-driven failure or pass. All three named Failure techniques for this SC (F42, F54, F55) — the canonical hand-built failing-page recipes — have no analog in the corpus.

Application/domain monoculture: ~16 of 25 cases reuse one of two boilerplate bodies (the WCAG-abstract <section> or the srcdoc 'Home' link). No realistic content domain (e-commerce, forms, media player, navigation menu, data table, editor, map, game) appears.

Outcome skew toward inapplicable (16 inapplicable vs 6 pass vs 3 fail), and the inapplicable cases are dominated by CSS-edge-cases (overflow:hidden/visible, scroll-distance < padding, 1x1 iframe, hidden iframe) — heavy investment in 'is the rule even triggered' boundary conditions rather than in true keyboard-operability variety.

Timing dimension (the SC's second normative clause) and the path-dependent exception (its only normative carve-out) are both completely untested, so a tool/judge could pass the entire corpus while having no signal on either normative limb.

Hover/tooltip essential-information and alternative-keyboard-mode reasoning (the two judgment-heavy parts of TT Test 4.A) are absent, so the corpus exercises none of the 'is the same function reachable another way' reasoning that real 2.1.1 evaluation requires.

No dynamic/interaction-state variety: nothing requires actually pressing a key and observing a state change; cases are statically decidable from DOM+CSS, which is why both rules are auto/semi-auto — the corpus inherits and reinforces that static bias rather than probing genuine keyboard interaction.

aspects.title: Pointer-only (mouse/touch/gesture) handlers on non-native elements with no keyboard equivalent (F54)
aspects.description: A function is wired up exclusively through pointing-device events (onclick/onmousedown/onmouseup/onmouseover, or touch/pointer/gesture listeners) on an element that has no native keyboard behaviour and no tabindex, role, or key handler — typically a div, span, img, li, or svg. The page looks fully operable, but a keyboard-only user can never reach or invoke the function. The human-judgment core is recognizing that a given visual control (a 'Next' arrow image, a star-rating widget, a custom 'Add to cart' tile, a swipeable carousel) actually IS interactive functionality whose only trigger is a pointer event — i.e. mapping pixels-that-do-something to the absence of any keyboard path — then confirming there is no keyboard route anywhere on the page. This is the canonical F54 failure and the core of Trusted Tester's 'use the mouse to determine available functions, then operate them with the keyboard' procedure.
aspects.scLimb: 2.1.1 'all functionality is operable through a keyboard interface' — reachability AND activation of explicit/custom interactive controls (not scroll regions). Does not exercise the keystroke-timing limb. Also maps to 2.1.3.
aspects.whyUncovered: Neither ACT rule (0ssw9k scroll reachability, akn7bn iframe tab order) inspects element event handlers at all. The corpus contains zero pages where 'this thing does something on click but nothing on keyboard'. The judgment requires using the mouse to discover that a visually-styled element is functional and is semantic, not detectable by a static checker that has no concept of which non-native elements are 'meant' to be operable.

references.quote: When pointing device-specific event handlers are the only mechanism available to invoke a function of the content, users with no vision ... as well as users who must use alternate keyboards or input devices that act as keyboard emulators will be unable to access the function of the content.

Use the mouse/pointer to determine **available functions** provided by interactive elements (drop-down menus, form fields, revealing/hiding content, tooltips, AND all interactive interface components).

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build otherwise-accessible pages with one or more localized pointer-only controls so the failure is a semantic discovery, not a structurally broken page. Use non-native elements (div/span/img/li/svg) carrying onclick/onmousedown/touch/pointer listeners, no tabindex, no role, no key handler, and styled to look like real controls (cursor:pointer, hover effects). Mirror F54's exact example for at least one case. Include matched controls elsewhere on the page that ARE keyboard accessible, so the verdict turns on the one localized pointer-only affordance rather than a wholesale-broken page.
suggestedScenarios: A 5-star rating widget made of ★ elements, each with onclick that sets the rating — no tabindex, no role, no key handler; visually a normal rating control, keyboard-dead.
A product-card grid where each <div class="card" onclick="location.href='/product/123'"> navigates on click; cards behave like links under mouse but are unreachable by Tab.
An carousel arrow (mirroring F54) embedded in an otherwise accessible page, so the failure is one localized control.
A 'show more' expander as Show more ▾ with no tabindex; the only way to reveal hidden content is a mouse click.
A colour-swatch picker (<li onclick="pick('red')">) where choosing a variant is mouse-only, while the rest of the checkout form is keyboard accessible.
A custom slider built from a draggable <div> with onmousedown/onmousemove only (no arrow-key handling, no role=slider), so the value can be set by mouse drag but never by keyboard.

aspects.title: Emulated links/controls that are reachable but not truly activatable by keyboard — wrong element, Enter-only, or no-op handler (F42)
aspects.description: The subtle slice between a bare pointer-only fake control and a properly built one. Markup that reads as compliant (tabindex present, an onkeypress/onkeydown attribute present, role=button/link) but where keyboard ACTIVATION silently fails: (a) a <div tabindex=0 onclick> with no key handler at all — focusable, so it appears 'in the tab order', but Enter/Space do nothing because a div has no implicit activation; (b) an onkeypress that listens ONLY for Enter (keyCode 13) while onclick does the work, so Space (and any keydown-only AT) gets nothing; (c) a handler that calls preventDefault/returns early on keyboard, swallowing activation; (d) an <a> WITHOUT href (just onclick) that drops out of the tab order entirely despite looking like a real link in source. F42 only fails 2.1.1 when keyboard activation actually fails — so the human must FOCUS the element and actually PRESS the key, in both Enter and Space, rather than trust the presence of attributes.
aspects.scLimb: 2.1.1 'operable through a keyboard interface' — specifically the activation half (reach-AND-execute). The note in Understanding that a custom button reacting only to Enter still passes makes this a genuine judgment call, not a mechanical rule. Also maps to 2.1.3.
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus has no scripted-control cases at all; its only 'pass via focusable descendant' uses a genuine native <a href>. There is no case where a fake control is keyboard-reachable-but-not-activatable, no Enter-only/Space-missing handler, and no href-less anchor — so the activation-verification dimension is entirely untested. A static checker sees tabindex+role+a key listener and reads it as compliant; only behavioural key-press verification reveals the gap.

references.quote: This failure occurs when JavaScript event handlers are attached to elements to emulate links. A link created in this manner cannot be tabbed to from the keyboard and does not gain keyboard focus like other controls and/or links.
Use the keyboard to operate identified functionality and/or access the essential information: tab to the element and execute (e.g., press Enter with focus on the element).

aspects.constructionStrategy: Author matched pairs that look identical in source but diverge under actual key presses. Vary one mechanism at a time: present-but-no-op key handler, Enter-only handler, preventDefault-swallow, href-less anchor. Where useful, place a near-identical genuinely-operable sibling so the page's verdict hinges on actually pressing Enter AND Space, not on attribute presence. Keep the rest of the page keyboard-accessible to isolate the activation defect.
suggestedScenarios: A <div onclick="submit()" tabindex="0"> with NO key handler — focusable (reads as 'in tab order') but Enter/Space do nothing because a div has no implicit activation.

A <span role="link" tabindex="0" onclick="go()" onkeypress="if(event.key==='Enter')go()"> that works (pass) beside a sibling that drops the onkeypress (mouse-only fail) — a matched pair forcing the activation check.
A fake link with tabindex=0 and an onkeypress listening ONLY for keyCode 13 (Enter); pressing Space does nothing and there is no keydown handler — reachable but partially dead.
An made focusable via tabindex=0 whose onkeypress calls e.preventDefault() and returns early, swallowing activation while appearing wired up.
A toolbar of <a> elements WITHOUT href (just onclick) — anchors with no href are not focusable, so they look like real links in source but drop out of the tab order.
A 'menu' of <div role="button"> items, focusable with onclick, whose onkeyup checks window.event.keyCode (undefined in browsers that only populate the event argument), so activation silently fails.

aspects.title: Drag-and-drop / endpoint-style functions without the path exception, lacking a keyboard equivalent (G90 / G202 / Understanding)
aspects.description: The SC exempts only functions whose input depends on the PATH of movement, not just the endpoints (free-hand drawing, watercolour). Reordering a list by drag, dragging a file into a dropzone, sorting kanban cards, dragging a map pin, or resizing a panel are endpoint-dependent and therefore do NOT qualify for the exception — they REQUIRE a keyboard equivalent (cut/paste, move up/down buttons, an 'enter position' field, type-to-set coordinates). Two human judgments no checker can make: (1) decide whether a given drag operation is genuinely path-dependent (exempt) or merely endpoint-dependent (must be keyboard-operable) — a semantic call about the underlying function; and (2) determine whether SOME keyboard alternative for the same function exists ANYWHERE on the page, since G202/Understanding allow a separate keyboard mode rather than per-control parity. A drag-to-reorder list with no up/down buttons fails; the same list WITH up/down buttons passes — identical drag markup, opposite verdicts.
aspects.scLimb: 2.1.1 'all functionality is operable through a keyboard interface' at the FUNCTION level, plus the path-vs-endpoint EXCEPTION clause — the only part of the SC's normative text that carves out functionality. G202's 'multiple methods to perform the same function' is the parity-not-per-control allowance.
aspects.whyUncovered: There is no drag-and-drop, sorting, resizing, or dropzone case anywhere in the 2.1.1 corpus. The exception clause (path of movement vs endpoints) is never exercised, and the 'keyboard alternative exists elsewhere on the page' allowance is never modeled. Both ACT rules check single-control reachability, not function-level keyboard parity, and a checker cannot reason about whether a drag is path- or endpoint-dependent.

references.quote: Drawing straight lines, regular geometric shapes, re-sizing windows and dragging objects to a location (when the path to that location is not relevant) do not require path dependent input.
This does not necessarily mean that each of the individual controls can be used from the keyboard as long as there are multiple methods to perform the same function available on the page.
make sure that all event handlers triggered by non-keyboard UI events are also associated with a keyboard-based event, or provide redundant keyboard-based mechanisms to accomplish the functionality

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build endpoint-dependent drag interactions (HTML5 draggable=true + dragstart/drop, or pointer-driven move) and toggle the presence of a keyboard alternative to create fail/pass matched pairs. Include at least one legitimate path-dependent EXCEPTION case (free-hand canvas) that must NOT be flagged, to test correct application of the exemption. For parity cases, place the keyboard equivalent visibly elsewhere on the page so the verdict turns on function-level reasoning, not per-control reachability.
suggestedScenarios: A to-do list reorderable only by HTML5 drag-and-drop (draggable=true + dragstart/drop), no up/down buttons — fails: the endpoint-only reorder has no keyboard route.
The SAME to-do list WITH 'Move up'/'Move down' <button>s beside each item — passes (keyboard equivalent for the same function exists elsewhere), forcing the parity judgment.
A file-upload dropzone that ONLY accepts dragged files (drop handler) and hides any <input type=file> — fails; a variant that keeps a visible/clickable file input passes.
A kanban board where cards move between columns by mouse drag only — endpoint-dependent (no path exception), confirm no keyboard move control exists.
A free-hand signature/drawing <canvas> capturing mousemove strokes — legitimately invokes the path-dependent EXCEPTION and must NOT be flagged.
A two-pane splitter resizable by dragging the divider with no arrow-key handler on role=separator — endpoint-relevant, needs keyboard control, fails without it.

aspects.title: Hover/pointer-only revealed content carrying essential information or controls, with no keyboard path (Trusted Tester essential-information branch)
aspects.description: Content or controls that appear only on mouseover/hover (CSS :hover dropdowns/megamenus, JS mouseover tooltips, hover-revealed action buttons on table rows or cards) with no focus/keyboard trigger and no equivalent elsewhere. Trusted Tester explicitly splits the SC into operable-functionality AND access-to-essential-information, and gives the precise tooltip nuance: place keyboard focus and if the information does not appear within two seconds, keyboard focus will not reveal it — then ask whether that information is available elsewhere on the page. Two human judgments: (1) is the hover-revealed content merely decorative/redundant (no failure) or does it carry ESSENTIAL information or the only access to a function (failure if keyboard can't get it AND it's not elsewhere)?; (2) does focus actually reveal the same content that hover does? Both demand reasoning about meaning and interacting in two modalities. Distinct from 1.4.13's persistence/dismissal requirements — this is purely about keyboard reachability of the function/info.
aspects.scLimb: 2.1.1 'all functionality is operable through a keyboard interface' AND the essential-information access branch, with the 'available elsewhere on the page' allowance. The essential-vs-decorative call and the two-second title-reveal check are the human-judgment core.
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus has no hover-revealed menus, tooltips, or row-action affordances, and never models the 'essential information available elsewhere' allowance. 0ssw9k/akn7bn never inspect :hover or mouseover content. The essential-vs-decorative distinction and the two-second title-reveal check are wholly absent, and neither is decidable by a static checker (it cannot judge whether hidden text is 'essential' or redundant).

references.quote: Use the mouse to identify instances where interactive elements provide **information essential** to understanding or operating page content.
For interactive elements with `title` attributes, place keyboard focus; if the tooltip does not appear within **two seconds**, keyboard focus will not reveal the title information.
If an element does not provide access to essential information via keyboard, determine whether the information is **available elsewhere** on the page (e.g., as text).

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build hover-only reveals (CSS :hover with no :focus-within; JS mouseover with no focus handler; title attributes with no aria-describedby) and vary whether the revealed payload is essential and whether it is duplicated elsewhere on the page, to produce both fail and pass verdicts. Cover both content-reveal (essential info) and control-reveal (the only access to a function). Include a case where focus DOES reveal the same content (pass) to test the modality-equivalence check.
suggestedScenarios: A nav with CSS :hover-only submenus (ul li:hover > ul) and no :focus-within / JS focus handling — submenu links unreachable by keyboard; essential navigation lost.
A data table where each row's 'Edit/Delete' buttons are display:none until the row is :hover-ed — keyboard users can never reach the only controls to act on a row.
A pricing tile whose only explanation of a plan limit is a JS mouseover tooltip that never fires on focus, with the text appearing nowhere else — essential info inaccessible by keyboard.
The SAME tooltip case but with the explanatory text ALSO present as visible body copy below — passes via 'available elsewhere on the page', forcing the redundancy judgment.
A control whose title attribute holds essential instructions; on keyboard focus no tooltip appears within two seconds and there is no aria-describedby — fails the essential-info branch.
An image hotspot that reveals part details on mouseover only (onmouseover swaps a caption), with no focusable hotspots — keyboard users get no part information.

aspects.title: Scripts that remove or steal focus the moment it is received (F55) — focus cannot rest on a control
aspects.description: Content that would normally receive focus has that focus stripped by script (onfocus="this.blur()", a handler that immediately moves focus elsewhere, or a focusin listener that bounces focus back to the top on every Tab). The element appears in the tab order and is technically reachable, but focus cannot remain on it long enough to operate it, so keyboard operation is impossible. This is dynamic behaviour: the static DOM shows a normal, well-formed, focusable control — only by actually tabbing through and watching where focus lands does a human discover focus being yanked away. The judgment is temporal/behavioural: 'I pressed Tab, the indicator flashed on the field, then jumped away.' Real-world variants include an overlay that re-focuses its first element on every focusin, or a sticky-header script that re-focuses the logo whenever a lower control gains focus.
aspects.scLimb: 2.1.1 'operable through a keyboard interface' — the persistence dimension: reachable is necessary but not sufficient; focus must be able to REST so the control can be operated. Orthogonal to scroll-region/iframe reachability.
aspects.whyUncovered: 0ssw9k only checks whether a tab stop EXISTS on/within a scroll region; it never checks whether focus can persist there. akn7bn checks iframe tab inclusion. Nothing in the corpus runs a focus-event handler or models focus being removed after receipt, so the 'reachable but focus won't stay' failure has zero coverage. Detecting it requires running the page and observing focus movement — a behavioural trace, not static markup analysis.

references.quote: Content that normally receives focus when the content is accessed by keyboard may have this focus removed by scripting. ... this practice removes focus from the content entirely, which means that the content can only be operated by a pointing device such as a mouse.
Check that when focus is placed on each element, focus remains there until user moves it.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Author normal, well-formed focusable controls and attach focus-stealing scripts so the defect is purely behavioural. Vary the mechanism: inline onfocus=this.blur() (mirroring F55), deferred setTimeout blur, focus moved to another element, and a page-wide focusin handler that re-focuses the masthead. Keep the static markup clean so the failure is only discoverable by tabbing and tracing where focus lands. Where useful, leave the rest of the page operable to isolate the affected control(s).
suggestedScenarios: A login form whose submit <input type="submit" onfocus="this.blur()"> mirrors F55 — focus reaches it then instantly leaves, so it can never be activated by keyboard.
A search field with onfocus calling document.body.focus(), so every attempt to tab in bounces focus to the body; the field is in source but uneditable by keyboard.
A page-wide addEventListener('focusin', e => header.focus()) that yanks focus to the masthead logo whenever any downstream control is focused, trapping the user near the top.
A custom dropdown whose options each have onfocus re-focusing the trigger button, so arrow/tab into the list immediately rebounds.
A 'newsletter' overlay that on any focusin re-focuses its first input, making it impossible to Tab to the close button or out of the overlay.
A control with onfocus="setTimeout(()=>this.blur(),0)" (deferred blur) — less obvious in source but still strips focus on every visit.

aspects.title: Keystroke-timing dependence: functions that require specific timing of individual keystrokes (Test 4.B / second SC limb)
aspects.description: The second normative limb of 2.1.1: 'without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes.' A function may be fully keyboard-reachable and activatable yet still FAIL because it demands a timing of keystrokes that keyboard-interface users (especially speech-input, sip-and-puff, switch, and on-screen-keyboard users) cannot reliably produce: keys that must be held down for an extended period before registering, multiple keystrokes that must be entered within a short window, double-press/rapid-repeat shortcuts with a tight interval, or input where the speed/rhythm of typing is itself part of the function (e.g. keystroke-dynamics 'authentication'). Understanding gives the exact examples. The judgment is behavioural and temporal — a human must notice that activation depends on HOW FAST or HOW LONG keys are pressed, not merely on WHICH keys. Per Test 4.B, a pass is still possible if another keyboard-accessible method on the page does not require specific timing.
aspects.scLimb: 2.1.1 second limb — 'without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes.' This limb is entirely separate from the operability limb both ACT rules target; Trusted Tester isolates it as Test 4.B.
aspects.whyUncovered: Both ACT rules (scroll reachability, iframe tab order) test only the operability limb and never the timing limb. There is no corpus case where a control activates only with a held key, a rapid key sequence, or speed-of-typing input. A static checker cannot infer timing requirements from markup; this requires observing time-dependent input behaviour, and judging whether an untimed keyboard alternative exists elsewhere.

references.quote: Examples of "specific timings for individual keystrokes" include situations where a user would be required to repeat or execute multiple keystrokes within a short period of time or where a key must be held down for an extended period before the keystroke is registered.

Determine whether there are instances where the **timing of keystrokes** is required to activate the element (e.g., the speed at which password keystrokes are typed is part of password authentication).
If timing-dependent functionality exists, determine if another keyboard-accessible method on the page does **not** require specific timing.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Implement controls whose activation depends on keystroke timing (keydown duration, inter-keystroke interval, double-press window, or typing cadence captured by JS) so the page is keyboard-reachable but timing-gated. Mirror Understanding's examples: hold-to-activate and burst-of-keystrokes. Include at least one pass case where an untimed keyboard alternative for the same function is provided elsewhere on the page, to exercise the Test 4.B allowance. Keep activation otherwise keyboard-operable so the verdict isolates the timing limb.
suggestedScenarios: A 'delete account' button that only fires if the Enter key is HELD for 2+ seconds (keydown/keyup duration check) — fails the timing limb; a tap of Enter does nothing.
A keyboard shortcut requiring a rapid double-press of a key within 300ms to trigger an action, with no single-press alternative — fails for users who cannot press that fast.
A password/PIN field whose JS measures inter-keystroke speed as part of 'authentication', rejecting input typed slowly — mirrors the TT example; fails.
A game-like control where an action only registers if a sequence of keys is entered within a short window — timing-dependent activation with no untimed path.
A 'press and hold to confirm' Space-activated control — fails; a sibling page adds a plain Enter-to-confirm button (untimed alternative) and passes, exercising the Test 4.B allowance.
A carousel that advances only on rapid repeated arrow-key presses (debounced to require fast repeats) with no single-press 'next' control.

pages.mechanism: Taken alone each <li onclick> is the F54 shape (pointer-only, no tabindex/role/keydown), but 2.1.1 asks whether the FUNCTION is keyboard operable, not whether every visible control is focusable. The colour-selection function is fully available from the keyboard via the labelled <select> (in tab order, arrow/typeahead operable, calls the same pickColour()), and the chips are aria-hidden so screen-reader users use the menu. Because an equivalent keyboard method for the same action exists, this passes 2.1.1 — demonstrating that a pointer-only handler is not automatically a failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the inverse trap for automation: a naive heuristic flagging '<li> onclick with no keyboard handler' would FALSE-POSITIVE here, while scanners that ignore the chips report nothing. Neither can perform the deciding judgment — recognising the chips are an F54-shaped control AND that the adjacent <select> provides the equivalent keyboard route for the same function, so no failure exists. pages.scenario: Webmail reading-pane message-action toolbar (Reply, Reply all, Forward, Archive, Delete) built from <a class=action onclick> anchors that have NO href and no tabindex. Core message actions are therefore keyboard-unreachable. Verified: calling .focus() on a toolbar anchor does not make it activeElement; 30 Tab presses from body never land on .msg-toolbar a.action.

pages.scenario: Museum virtual-exhibitions gallery where each clickable cover enters a virtual room. Each has onclick AND an onkeypress, so it appears keyboard-wired, but the handleKey handler calls event.preventDefault() and returns false BEFORE any activation branch — so for every key, including Enter and Space, it stops default behaviour and exits without calling enterRoom(). The key handler is present but swallows activation; no fallback control exists.
pages.mechanism: The element is focusable with a button role and accessible name (alt) and has an onkeypress, so all static keyboard signals are satisfied. But the handler body does event.preventDefault(); return false; making the if(Enter/Space) enterRoom() branch unreachable, so the dialog never opens from the keyboard. Mouse onclick is untouched. Verified: Enter-activates=false, Space-activates=false, mouse-click=true.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every static signal — tabindex=0, role=button, alt name, onclick, AND onkeypress — says 'focusable, named, keyboard handler present', satisfying 'interactive element must have a keyboard handler' heuristics. The defect is entirely in the runtime control flow of the handler (preventDefault + early return before activation). No static analyzer evaluates handler bodies to prove the activation branch is unreachable; only pressing Enter/Space and watching the room never open reveals it.

pages.scenario: Cloud-console deployments table where each row has a 'more actions' kebab built as <div role=button tabindex=0 aria-haspopup aria-expanded onclick onkeydown>. The bug is a semantic error inside the handler (reading charCode, which is 0 on keydown). pages.scenario: Credit-union online-banking sign-in form. The username/password fields are operable, but the primary submit control carries onfocus="this.blur()" (the canonical F55 one-liner). A keyboard user can Tab to the Sign in button but focus is stripped the instant it lands, throwing focus to <body>, so the button can never be activated by keyboard.
pages.mechanism: Inline onfocus HTML event-handler attribute on a native <input type=submit> synchronously calls this.blur() when the element receives focus, so focus is removed on receipt and relocated to document.body; the named, focusable control cannot retain focus to be operated.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: In a static DOM snapshot the submit button is a valid, named, focusable native control with no missing/empty attributes. The defect is purely behavioural: it only manifests when the focus event fires at runtime and the handler blurs the element. No static rule dispatches focus to each control and re-reads document.activeElement after the event loop turns; an onfocus attribute is not itself an error, so its presence cannot be flagged. Verified with Puppeteer: focusing input.signin leaves activeElement=body.

pages.scenario: German municipal services portal (de-DE). The site-search field has a mis-wired 'select on focus' helper whose early-return branch calls document.body.focus(). Because the box ships with a remembered query, the buggy branch fires on the first focus: every Tab into the search field bounces focus to <body> (made focusable via script-set tabindex=-1), so a keyboard user can never land in the box to type.
pages.mechanism: An onfocus handler relocates focus to a different, non-operable element (document.body, programmatically focusable via tabindex=-1) on receipt, conditional on the field holding its remembered value; the labelled type=search input cannot retain focus so free-text search is not keyboard-executable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Scanners see a correctly labelled type=search input and a valid submit button — zero markup errors. The focus theft only occurs at runtime when the focus event fires AND the field still holds its remembered value (stateful, conditional). A linter cannot know the helper calls document.body.focus() nor that body was made focusable via a script-set tabindex; there is no static signature for 'focus moves to body on receipt'. pages.scenario: Newspaper article page with a sticky masthead. A page-wide document focusin listener re-focuses the masthead logo on every focus change ('keep the brand the anchor'), and its exclusion guard compares the wrong property so it never excludes anything. Every Tab to a section-nav link, an article-tool button, the newsletter field, or an in-article link snaps focus back to the logo, freezing the whole page at the masthead for keyboard users.

pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The DOM is exemplary — semantic header/nav, real <a>/<button>, a labelled email input — so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse find no errors. pages.scenario: E-commerce storefront newsletter overlay (role=dialog, aria-modal). A marketing-popup plugin's focus management is a modal-scoped focusin listener that re-focuses the email input on every focus-in, with no exclusion for Close (x), the decline link, or Submit. A keyboard user can never Tab off the email field: every attempt to reach Close/Submit rebounds to the email box, so the overlay can neither be dismissed nor submitted by keyboard.
pages.mechanism: A modal-scoped focusin listener defers (setTimeout 0) and re-focuses a single element (the first input) on every focus-in, so the dismiss/submit controls receive focus momentarily then have it stripped and re-granted to the email field. This is a 2.1.1 'focus cannot rest' failure (focus actively relocated to one element), distinct from a 2.1.2 Tab-cycle trap.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The static markup is a well-formed dialog (role=dialog, aria-modal, aria-labelledby, named Close button, labelled email input) so scanners report nothing. pages.scenario: SaaS analytics dashboard with a custom APG 'Date range' listbox (role=button trigger + role=listbox/option, correct aria-expanded/aria-selected, full Arrow/Enter/Escape). It opens by keyboard, but each option has a deferred self-blur added to fix a flicker: on the option's focus event a setTimeout(0) later calls opt.blur() then trigger.focus(). The ring flashes on an option then snaps back to the trigger, so no option can be selected by keyboard.
pages.mechanism: A per-option focus handler asynchronously (setTimeout 0) blurs the option and re-focuses the trigger on every option focus, so options are reachable via Arrow keys but focus is removed on receipt and relocated to the trigger — no option can retain focus to be activated/selected by keyboard.

The focus theft is deferred inside a runtime focus handler, so there is no inline onfocus=this.blur() to grep and even a synchronous post-focus() snapshot still shows the option focused — you must wait an event-loop turn and re-read activeElement. pages.scenario: Rich-text document-editor toolbar over a contenteditable. Each formatting button declines focus ONLY on pointer interaction via mousedown -> e.preventDefault() (the standard pattern that keeps the caret in the editor when you click Bold). There is no onfocus=this.blur() and no focusin re-grab: a keyboard user can Tab to every button, focus RESTS on it, and Space/Enter toggles aria-pressed. Boundary variant proving mouse-only focus suppression is not F55.
pages.mechanism: mousedown -> preventDefault() cancels the default MOUSE focus assignment only (it fires on physical pointer press, never on Tab), so keyboard focus is never removed: focus lands on the toolbar button and remains, and the click handler toggles aria-pressed. F55's passing condition ('focus remains there until user moves it') holds for the keyboard path.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This tests the inverse error: a tool or reviewer that flagged anything resembling focus suppression near preventDefault would FALSELY fail this page. Tools cannot tell from static markup whether the suppression affects keyboard focus or only pointer focus — distinguishing a mousedown-scoped preventDefault() (legitimate) from a focus/focusin self-blur (F55) requires running the page and tracing focus. Verified with Puppeteer: focusing the Bold button leaves activeElement on that button after the event-loop turn (focus rests).

pages.scenario: Public-transit trip planner with a route map. Speech-input (one key at a time), switch/scanning (slow cadence), tremor, and on-screen-keyboard users cannot produce a sub-250 ms double-press, and no single-press/untimed alternative exists.
